situation:
You and your teammate are the director of customer experience and the director of store operations at MAPLERIDGE HOME LEASING, a rent-to-own retailer that furnishes homes and appliances under weekly agreements. The chief executive officer (judge) leads the company. MAPLERIDGE has grown over close to fifteen years into the largest rent-to-own chain in its state, and it is now preparing to open its first showrooms across the state line.

MAPLERIDGE built that lead on plain dealing. Every agreement carries a printed promise, repeated in the company's advertising, that no term will change until customers have been told a full billing quarter in advance. Associates quote that promise from memory, and many of them answer customer questions from their personal social media accounts, on their own time and in their own words.

The flagship showroom's café functions as more than a break room. It hosts the weekend account clinics where customers bring in paperwork they do not understand, it serves the surrounding neighborhood at lunch, and it is where associates hear first when a policy lands badly. Whatever the company decides here will be explained across those tables long before it reaches a corporate statement.

A national leasing platform has offered MAPLERIDGE the underwriting reach and the account system the out-of-state showrooms require. The operator will admit one regional chain to that market this season, and it requires every current customer moved onto its own terms of service before the first new showroom opens, well inside the notice window MAPLERIDGE promised.

Accepting means telling long-standing customers that the promise printed on their agreements is being shortened, and letting associates learn of it alongside them. Holding to the full notice period keeps that promise, but the platform's window closes, the out-of-state showrooms are postponed, and the associates already offered transfers and management roles at those showrooms stay where they are.

The chief executive officer (judge) wants your team to recommend how much notice the change should carry, how it should be delivered to customers and to associates, and what guidance associates should have about discussing it on their personal accounts. The chief executive officer (judge) will greet your team and ask to hear your ideas. After your presentation and questions, the chief executive officer (judge) will thank your team for the work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the chief executive officer (judge) of MAPLERIDGE HOME LEASING. Business background is the same as the situation above. You must decide how much notice the change to the terms of service will carry, how customers and associates will be told, and what associates may say about it on their personal accounts, and you have asked the director of customer experience and the director of store operations to recommend a course of action.

You will greet the participant team and ask to hear their ideas. After the team has presented, you will ask the following questions:
judgeQuestions: A year from now, how do you think customers will describe the way we told them?
Once the new showrooms are open, what happens if associates keep answering questions about this on their own accounts?
